interviewQuestions.question: Design the news feed ranking system for a social app.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start by clarifying scale and latency — assume hundreds of millions of daily feed loads, sub-300ms end-to-end. That immediately implies a multi-stage funnel rather than one model scoring everything.

**Candidate generation**: pull a few hundred posts per user from people/pages they follow plus a recommended pool, using a cheap retrieval method so it's feasible per-request at this scale.

**Ranking**: score that shortlist with a model using user, content, and — most valuable — cross features (this user's history with this specific author/topic). I wouldn't train on a single label; I'd predict several engagement proxies (like, comment, share, watch-time) and combine them, since any single proxy alone gets gamed or misrepresents true value — raw engagement optimization specifically breeds outrage-bait.

**Re-ranking**: apply freshness decay and diversity caps (no more than 2 consecutive posts from one author) as an explicit rule layer on top of the relevance score, since that's easier to tune than teaching a model the property implicitly.

I'd close on evaluation and monitoring: offline NDCG/precision@k as a cheap filter, then an A/B test on retention and meaningful-interaction rate — not just engagement — before shipping, plus drift monitoring since content and user behavior both shift over time.

**Testing:** whether you can integrate ranking, label design, and business-rule layering into one coherent answer instead of only naming a model.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Feed ranking system design

interviewQuestions.question: Why does feed ranking use a multi-stage funnel instead of one model scoring every candidate post directly?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The blocking constraint is scale versus latency: a user might have millions of candidate posts available across everyone they follow plus a recommendation pool, and the feed has to render in well under a second. Running one rich model — the kind that uses deep cross-features between the specific user and specific content — over millions of candidates per request simply isn't computationally feasible at that latency budget, no matter how much hardware you throw at it; the cost scales with the candidate count, and that count is too large for an expensive model to touch directly.

The funnel resolves this by matching each stage's cost to how much precision it actually needs to provide. Candidate generation uses a cheap method (often a fast embedding lookup) to narrow millions of posts down to a few hundred plausible ones — it doesn't need to get the exact best posts, just to reliably avoid throwing away good ones, since anything wrongly discarded here never gets a second chance. Ranking then applies the expensive model, but only to that few-hundred-post shortlist, which is computationally tractable within the latency budget. Re-ranking applies cheap rule-based adjustments (diversity, freshness) to the already-scored top results, since those don't need a learned model at all.

The core principle: each stage should be exactly as accurate as it needs to be to hand a good-enough shortlist downstream, not maximally accurate — spending model capacity uniformly across millions of candidates when only a few hundred will ever be shown is wasted compute that a smart architect should reallocate to the stage that actually determines what the user sees.

**Testing:** whether you can justify the funnel architecture from a genuine compute/latency constraint, not just describe it as a standard pattern to recite.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why the multi-stage funnel exists

interviewQuestions.question: Your feed's A/B test shows a new ranking model increases engagement metrics significantly, but a follow-up study three months later shows retention actually declined. How do you diagnose and prevent this?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
This is the engagement-optimization trap showing up with a delay, and it's exactly why short-term proxy metrics and long-run business goals can diverge — the model was trained and evaluated against engagement proxies (clicks, likes, comments, watch-time) as a stand-in for "the feed is good for the user," and it's entirely possible to win on those proxies in the short term while degrading what actually matters, because nothing in the training objective directly represented long-term user well-being or retention.

My diagnosis would start by segmenting the engagement lift: is it concentrated in content types associated with outrage, sensationalism, or compulsive-but-unsatisfying engagement (doomscrolling patterns, content the user later reports as "not worth their time" if surveyed)? If the lift traces heavily to that kind of content, it strongly supports the hypothesis that the model learned to amplify engagement-maximizing-but-value-destroying content, exactly the failure mode raw engagement optimization tends toward, since the model has no notion of "valuable" beyond whatever proxy it was given.

The structural fix isn't reverting the model and giving up the engagement win outright — it's changing what the model is actually optimizing for. I'd push for labels further downstream of raw engagement: explicit surveys ("was this post worth your time"), and critically, training or at least evaluating against a metric that predicts long-run retention specifically, not just immediate-session engagement, since a model optimized purely for the latter has a direct incentive to trade future retention for present clicks. I'd also add an explicit downweighting or filtering layer for borderline-policy or known-outrage-pattern content regardless of how well it scores on engagement, as a guardrail independent of what the model learns.

**Testing:** whether you connect a short-term engagement win with a long-term retention loss to proxy-metric divergence specifically, and propose fixing the label/objective rather than just reverting the launch.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Diagnosing an engagement-retention divergence
